summary: A monarchy in the northwest corner of the Persian Gulf with abundant oil reserves, invaded by Iraq in 1990 and liberated the following year by a multinational coalition; foreign residents make up the majority of the population.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Kuwaiti citizens are almost all Muslim, mostly Sunni, with Shias making up about 30 percent of citizens, many of them descendants of merchant families who moved from Persia and Bahrain in the past. Because the foreign workforce also includes large numbers of Muslims from Egypt, Pakistan, Bangladesh and elsewhere, Islam is the country's largest religion, but its share is diluted by non-Muslim migrant workers to about three quarters.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Kuwait's native Christians number only a few hundred, mainly families who moved from Iraq, Turkey and the Levant in the early 20th century. The large number of Christians today are almost all foreign workers, including Catholic and Eastern-rite believers from Kerala in India, Filipino Catholics, and Egyptian Copts, with churches concentrated mainly in Kuwait City.

ranking.name: Other (Hinduism, Buddhism, etc.)
ranking.description: After Kuwait's oil boom of the 1970s it brought in large numbers of workers from South and Southeast Asia, among whom Hindus come from India and Nepal and Buddhists mostly from countries such as Sri Lanka and Thailand. They can practice their religion only in private places or in limited facilities, and their numbers vary with labor policy.

religion.background: The northeastern Arabian Peninsula, where Kuwait lies, was Islamized after the rise of Islam in the 7th century, while Failaka Island in the Persian Gulf preserves ancient Greek and early Christian sites. In the early 18th century tribes from the Arabian Peninsula settled here, around 1756 the Al-Sabah family became the rulers, in 1899 Kuwait became a British protectorate, and in 1961 it became independent. The constitution makes Islam the state religion and Islamic law one of the main sources of legislation. After oil was discovered in 1938 the economy took off and large numbers of foreign workers moved in, so that foreigners now make up about two thirds of the total population, bringing religious diversity including Christianity, Hinduism and Buddhism.

ranking.name: Arabic (Kuwaiti dialect)
ranking.description: Arabic is the mother tongue and sole official language of Kuwaiti citizens, and the Kuwaiti dialect belongs to Gulf Arabic, having absorbed Persian, Hindi and other vocabulary in the era of pearl diving and maritime trade. Because foreigners are the majority of the population, only about half actually have Arabic as a mother tongue, the rest being mostly migrant workers from other Arab countries.

ranking.name: Indian languages (Malayalam, Hindi, etc.)
ranking.description: Trade between Kuwait and India goes back to the era of pearl diving and sailing-ship trade, and the Indian rupee was even Kuwait's currency (until 1961). After the oil boom of the 1970s large numbers of Indian workers moved in, the most numerous being Malayalam speakers from Kerala, and Indians are now Kuwait's largest foreign community.

ranking.name: Tagalog
ranking.description: After the 1970s Filipino workers began to go in large numbers to the Gulf countries, working in domestic service, health care and services. Tagalog has therefore become an important immigrant language in Kuwait, used mainly among domestic workers and retail workers.

language.history: The language of Kuwait is Gulf Arabic, close to the dialects of neighboring eastern Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Qatar, and through long maritime trade it absorbed vocabulary from Persian, Hindi, Turkish and English. During the British protectorate of 1899–1961 English entered education and commerce. After the discovery of oil in 1938 and oil exports from the 1950s, the government brought in large numbers of foreign workers, and South Asian languages and Filipino can be heard everywhere in daily life. The constitution makes Arabic the official language, and schools and government use Modern Standard Arabic.

ranking.name: Machboos (spiced rice)
ranking.description: Chicken, lamb or fish stewed with spices (black lime, cinnamon, cardamom, saffron and others) and braised together with long-grain rice into a spiced rice dish; it is Kuwait's national dish.
ranking.history: Machboos is closely related to India's biryani, reflecting the centuries of maritime trade between Kuwait and India: Kuwaiti merchants sailed dhows carrying dates and horses to India and brought back rice and spices. Black lime (dried lime) comes from Oman. Before the oil era of the 1950s, machboos was the guest-hosting dish of wealthy merchant families, and today it is an essential dish for Kuwaiti family Friday lunches and festivals.

ranking.name: Harees (wheat and meat porridge)
ranking.description: Crushed wheat and meat (mostly chicken or lamb) are stewed for a long time and mashed into a porridge, topped with butter or sprinkled with cinnamon. It is creamy like porridge and mild in flavor, often sprinkled with sugar or eaten with cinnamon.
ranking.history: Harees is a long-established dish of the Arabian Peninsula, and a similar wheat-and-meat porridge already appears in the 10th-century Baghdadi cookbook Kitab al-Tabikh. In the Gulf region it is closely tied to Islamic festivals, made in large quantities especially at the breaking of the fast in Ramadan and during Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha, often shared among neighbors, and is also a traditional dish for entertaining guests.

ranking.name: Balaleet (sweet vermicelli)
ranking.description: Fine vermicelli sweetened with sugar, saffron, cardamom and rose water and stir-fried, topped with a layer of fried egg, eaten as breakfast. The combination of sweet noodles and savory egg has a distinctive taste, and it is a breakfast unique to the Gulf region.
ranking.history: Balaleet is a sweet-and-savory breakfast unique to the Persian Gulf region; the noodles came with trade, while the saffron and cardamom reflect long contact with Persia and India. The dish is especially common on the morning of Eid al-Fitr, enjoyed by the family together after the dawn prayer, and is regarded as one of the festival's symbolic foods.

ranking.name: Luqaimat
ranking.description: Small balls fried from yeast dough, crisp outside and soft inside, drizzled with date syrup or honey and sprinkled with sesame. The crust is crisp and the inside fluffy, with the aroma of cardamom and saffron.
ranking.history: Luqaimat means "small bites", and similar fried-dough sweets are already recorded in 13th-century Baghdadi recipes, with different versions throughout the Arab world. In Kuwait and other Gulf countries it is the most popular dessert after the evening fast-breaking in Ramadan, and is also often served to guests at weddings and family gatherings.

ranking.name: Arabic coffee
ranking.description: A pale golden coffee brewed from lightly roasted beans with plenty of cardamom, poured in small amounts into small cups for guests and eaten with dates. It is light with a spiced flavor, entirely different from strong Turkish coffee.
ranking.history: Coffee spread in the 15th century among Sufi mystics in Yemen and then throughout the Arabian Peninsula. The Bedouin and the Gulf region treat serving coffee as the core of hospitality etiquette: the host pours coffee with his right hand, and the guest shakes the cup to signal that no more is wanted. In the traditional Kuwaiti social hall (diwaniya), Arabic coffee is always present when men gather to discuss current affairs; "Arabic coffee", jointly nominated in 2015 by the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Oman and Qatar, was inscribed by UNESCO on the Intangible Cultural Heritage list, showing that it is a hospitality culture shared across the whole Gulf region.
